title: Reading Type Errors
summary: What tsc tells you, the five errors you will see every day, and fixing the cause instead of silencing it.

steps.title: Anatomy of a tsc error
body: Every TypeScript error has the same parts. This is what `tsc --noEmit` prints in CI and what your editor underlines:
```text
src/orders.ts:14:7 - error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
14   qty: row[1],
- **`src/orders.ts:14:7`**: file, line, column. Jump there first.
- **`TS2322`**: the error code. Search it when the message is unclear; the same code always means the same kind of mistake.
- **The message**: read it as "the value I found" versus "the type you promised". With a long message, the **last** indented line usually names the exact property that differs.
From this lesson on, **Check** runs `tsc --strict --noEmit` on your code before the tests. A type error fails the step with exactly this message, on your line.
| Code | Means | Usual cause |
| `TS2322` | a value does not fit the type of what it is assigned to | forgot to convert a string from a form or a file |
| `TS2345` | an argument does not fit the parameter | same, at a call |
| `TS2339` | that property does not exist on this type | using a member of only one side of a union |
| `TS18048` | `x` is possibly `undefined` | `find`, optional properties, `Map.get` |
| `TS7006` | parameter implicitly has an `any` type | missing annotation under `strict` |

steps.prompt: Match each error code to what it is telling you.
pairs: this argument is the wrong type for the parameter
this type has no such property
a parameter has no type and `strict` will not guess `any`
this value cannot be assigned to that type

steps.prompt: Which error does `tsc --strict` report on the last line?
code: type User = { id: number; name: string };
options: `TS2339: Property 'name' does not exist on type 'User'.`
`TS2322: Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'User'.`
steps.explain: `find` returns `User | undefined`: there may be no match. Under `strict` (which turns on `strictNullChecks`) you must handle the `undefined` case before reading `.name`. Without that check this line would crash at run time with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`.

steps.title: Fix the cause, not the message
body: There are always two ways to make a type error go away. Only one is a fix.
```ts fragment
const user = users.find(u => u.id === id);
// Silencing: the crash is still there, you just told the compiler to stop looking.
user!.name;                  // non-null assertion
(user as User).name;         // cast
// @ts-ignore
// Fixing: handle the case the compiler found.
if (!user) return "unknown";     // narrow: below this line user is a User
user?.email ?? "no email";       // optional chaining with a fallback

In review, `!`, `as` and `@ts-ignore` need a reason in a comment. The one place they belong is at a **trust boundary** you have already checked, or in tests: `// @ts-expect-error` marks a line that **must** fail to compile, and becomes an error itself (`TS2578`) if it ever compiles. That is how library authors test their types.

steps.title: TS18048: possibly undefined
prompt: CI fails on this file with:
Fix `emailDomain(id)` so it type checks: return the part after `@` of the user's email, or `"unknown"` when there is no such user or the user has no email. Do not use `!`, `as` or `@ts-ignore`.
starter: type User = { id: number; name: string; email?: string };
const users: User[] = [{ id: 1, name: "Ada", email: "ada@example.org" }, { id: 2, name: "Lin" }];
solution: type User = { id: number; name: string; email?: string };
const users: User[] = [{ id: 1, name: "Ada", email: "ada@example.org" }, { id: 2, name: "Lin" }];

forbid.message: Does not use a non-null assertion (!)

hints: After `if (!user) return ...`, TypeScript knows `user` is a `User`.
`email` is optional, so check it too: `if (!user || !user.email) return "unknown";`
steps.explain: Narrowing with an early return is the everyday fix: the compiler follows the control flow, so after the check both `user` and `user.email` are known to exist. The `!` version would compile and still crash for user 2.

steps.title: TS2322: strings from a file
prompt: `parseLine` reads one CSV row like `"A-100,2,350"` (SKU, quantity, price in cents). `tsc` says:
main.ts(6,29): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
main.ts(6,39): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
Everything read from text is a string until you convert it. Fix `parseLine` so it type checks and returns real numbers. If a quantity or price is not a whole number, throw an `Error`.
starter: type Line = { sku: string; qty: number; priceCents: number };
return { sku: sku.trim(), qty: qty, priceCents: price };
solution: type Line = { sku: string; qty: number; priceCents: number };
if (text.trim() === "" || !Number.isInteger(n)) throw new Error("not a whole number: " + text);
return { sku: sku.trim(), qty: toInt(qty), priceCents: toInt(price) };
template: Dojo.throws("a price of '3.5' is rejected", () => parseLine("B,1,3.5"));
Dojo.throws("a missing quantity is rejected", () => parseLine("B,,10"));
hints: Write a small `toInt(text: string): number` helper and use it for both fields.
steps.explain: Without types, `"2" * "350"` would even work (JavaScript converts for `*`), but `"2" + "350"` gives `"2350"`. The compiler caught a bug class, and the conversion is also the right place to validate.

steps.prompt: A teammate silenced the compiler with `as any`. Node strips types and runs it anyway. What does it print?
code: const qty: number = input as any;
steps.explain: Types are erased: at run time `qty` is still the string `"5"`, and `"5" + 1` is `"51"`. `as any` turned a compile error into a wrong answer in production. This is why reviewers push back on casts.

steps.title: satisfies: checked, but not widened
prompt: The route table below is annotated `Record<string, Route>`. That checks every entry, but it also **widens** the keys to `string`, so `routeFor("acount")` (a typo) compiles and crashes at run time.
Change the declaration to use `satisfies Record<string, Route>` instead. Then:
- every entry is still checked against `Route` (a typo in `auth` is an error), and
- `keyof typeof routes` is exactly `"home" | "account" | "orders"`, so a wrong route name is a compile error.
The tests include a line marked `// @ts-expect-error` that calls `routeFor("acount")`: it must fail to compile.
starter: type Route = { path: string; auth: boolean };
function routeFor(name: keyof typeof routes): string {
solution: type Route = { path: string; auth: boolean };
function routeFor(name: keyof typeof routes): string {
hints: Remove the `: Record<string, Route>` annotation and put `satisfies Record<string, Route>` after the closing `}` of the object.
If the tests say `Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive` (TS2578), the keys are still widened to `string`.
steps.explain: An annotation decides the type; `satisfies` only checks against it and keeps what was inferred. Use it for config objects, route tables and lookup maps where you want both the check and the precise keys.
